Empirical Research Plan: Distributed Adaptive Meta-Heuristic Selection  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Randomized Controlled Experiment (Other)  

Why appropriate  
• The “data” are fully under the researcher’s control: for each independent run we can specify (i) which co-ordination rule the distributed system follows, (ii) the network topology, (iii) string length, λ, p_mut, etc.  
• Randomly assigning runs to the competing co-ordination rules guarantees ex-ante comparability; any difference in performance is therefore causally attributable to the rule.  
• Randomization is stronger than quasi-experimental DID/IV/RDD approaches and avoids their additional assumptions.  

Design details  
• Unit of randomization: an independent optimisation run (all nodes in that run use the same rule).  
• Factorial structure:  
  – Factor A (Treatment): Coordination rule ∈ {SBM-Distributed, Sequential-Adaptive, Naïve-Distributed}.  
  – Factor B (Topology): Complete, Grid, Cycle.  
  – Factor C (Size): n ∈ {4, 8, 16, 36, 64}.  
• 20 replications per cell ⇒ 3 × 3 × 5 × 20 = 900 runs.  
• Pre-specify random seeds for reproducibility and to allow re-shuffling tests.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if the run uses the Select-Best-and-Mutate (SBM) distributed rule (best neighbour + ε-exploration).  

Control groups  
Control 1: Sequential-Adaptive (single-processor reference implementation).  
Control 2: Naïve-Distributed (each node sticks to a fixed metaheuristic chosen uniformly at t = 0).  

Timing  
Since treatment is fixed from the first iteration, there is no staggered timing; each run is either treated or control throughout.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Successful randomization: assignment of runs to {Treated, Control 1, Control 2} is independent of potential outcomes.  
Plausibility: We programmatically randomise; fully satisfied.  

A2. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): outcomes of one run are unaffected by the rule used in another run.  
Plausibility: Each run is executed in an isolated process with its own RNG ⇒ holds.  

A3. Measurement validity: performance metrics (rounds, evaluations, messages) are recorded without error and identically across arms.  
Plausibility: Metrics are produced by the same logging library ⇒ credible.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Pseudo-random number generator correlation across runs  
• Mitigation: Use independent random seeds drawn from /dev/urandom; verify that results are unchanged when reseeding.  

T2. Lack of statistical power in small cells (e.g., n = 4, grid)  
• Mitigation: Ex-ante power calculation; increase replications or aggregate topology categories if needed.  

T3. Implementation bugs that differentially affect one algorithm  
• Mitigation: Code review, unit tests, and cross-checking simple cases (e.g., with λ = 1 the four rules should be identical).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Load required packages
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # efficient OLS / clustered SEs
library(clubSandwich) # CR2 robust variance
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data loading
# Assume each run written to one row in 'runs.csv'
# Columns: run_id, rule, topology, n_nodes, lambda, p_mut, 
#          rounds_to_opt, evals, msgs
dt <- fread("runs.csv")

# 2. Variable construction
dt[, treated := fifelse(rule == "SBM_Distributed", 1L, 0L)]
dt[, ctrl_seq  := fifelse(rule == "Sequential", 1L, 0L)]
dt[, ctrl_naive:= fifelse(rule == "Naive_Distributed", 1L, 0L)]

# 3. Main specification: compare SBM to pooled controls
# Outcome: rounds_to_opt (lower is better)
reg_main <- feols(rounds_to_opt ~ treated | topology + n_nodes, 
                  data = dt, vcov = ~topology)   # cluster by topology
summary(reg_main)

# 4. Robustness check 1: Include interaction with topology
reg_topo <- feols(rounds_to_opt ~ treated*topology | n_nodes, 
                  data = dt, vcov = ~topology)
summary(reg_topo)

# 5. Robustness check 2: Wild bootstrap for small clusters
library(fwildclusterboot)
boot_main <- boottest(reg_main, clustid = "topology", B = 999)
boot_main

# 6. Plot: distribution of outcomes by arm
ggplot(dt, aes(x = rounds_to_opt, fill = rule)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = .4) + theme_minimal()
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic (computational) intuition: SBM exploits the best operator observed locally while maintaining exploration, so it should converge faster than both controls, but especially outperform the naïve distributed rule.  
Prior: ‑15 % to ‑25 % fewer rounds to reach optimum relative to pooled controls, translating roughly to a coefficient of −150 to −250 rounds on a baseline mean of ~1000 rounds (exact magnitude will depend on l = 10 000).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Randomised Experiments)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Successful random assignment of treatment ………………… 1  
C2: Large enough sample / power …………………………………… 0.8  
C3: Low attrition / missing data ……………………………………… 1  
C4: No interference between units ………………………………… 1  
C5: Accurate, unbiased outcome measurement ………………… 1  

Total (out of 5) …………………………………………………… 4.8  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This design leverages full experimental control to deliver clean causal estimates of how much coordinated adaptive selection (SBM) improves distributed optimisation performance relative to realistic benchmarks.
